summary:
Meghālaya stands under India's national framework for every question that matters to a trans visitor: legal recognition, documents, entry, policing and remedies. Nothing in the sourced material identifies a Meghālaya-specific deviation from that national position, so the national assessment is the operative one here.

India's Parliament passed the Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Amendment Bill in March 2026. It strips the self-identification route from the 2019 law, limits legal recognition to historically accepted socio-cultural groups such as hijra and kinner plus intersex persons, and bases recognition on biological or physical traits. The measure reverses the 2014 Supreme Court ruling that had established self-identification as the standard. Trans men, trans women and non-binary people who self-identify outside the listed categories fall outside the recognition scheme.

Certification now runs through medical boards and district authorities, which must certify gender-affirming surgery before identity recognition is granted. A visitor whose documents predate this regime should expect documentary friction wherever recognition is tested.

The amendment also creates offences carrying up to life imprisonment for coercing or alluring anyone to be transgender. Human Rights Watch warned on 26 March 2026 that this provision could be used against support networks around trans people.

Presidential assent was still pending in late March 2026. Human Rights Watch urged the president not to sign the bill, and a Supreme Court-appointed advisory panel asked the government to withdraw it, calling the removal of self-identification a setback against the 2014 ruling.

The government presents the narrower definition as a way to target welfare benefits and anti-trafficking protection to a defined group. Critics, including rights activists, respond that it excludes many trans, non-binary and gender-fluid people; India is estimated to have around two million transgender people.

The entry and stay baseline is mixed. Same-sex acts were decriminalised by the Supreme Court in 2018 and discrimination is barred on grounds including sex, read to cover gender identity, but same-sex marriage and civil partnership are unavailable, although courts have acknowledged same-sex couples as family units.

Criminal-law protection weakened in 2024: replacing the Indian Penal Code with the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita removed the gender-identity-specific offences that had shielded trans people from sexual violence, and trans communities report fear of more assaults under the new code.

Documented exposure concentrates at checkpoints and in police contact. A trans woman alleged that a Railway Protection Force constable groped her under the pretext of a gender check at a Kolkata railway station; trans people arrested by the Railway Protection Force in Assam described degrading custody treatment in interviews recorded in June 2024. At Chennai International Airport Terminal 1 in November 2024, CISF personnel stopped the openly transgender law student Sakshi Jain even though she produced a PAN card. Passport authorities have required a trans applicant to undergo a medical examination, with the Allahabad High Court granting relief in February 2026.

The courts remain the strongest protection machinery. The Madras High Court judgment of 7 June 2021 in S. Sushma v Commissioner of Police, delivered by Justice N. Anand Venkatesh, followed police harassment of a same-sex couple and issued guidelines covering police sensitisation, a ban on conversion therapy and directions to the National Medical Commission and education authorities. The UK Home Office country note of December 2025 records only limited reports of police abuse of LGBT+ people, likelier in conservative rural areas and not systemic.

For a visitor the practical picture is narrowed recognition from March 2026, removed sexual-violence safeguards from 2024, documented abuse at railway, airport and passport encounters, and high courts that have repeatedly intervened on behalf of trans and LGBT+ people.
tangentialFactors:
The March 2026 amendment sits within a wider pattern of contested recognition rather than an isolated measure. Parliament's action followed years of litigation in which the Supreme Court and high courts expanded trans rights, and the Supreme Court's own advisory panel now opposes the government's bill. That tension between the legislature and the judiciary is likely to produce further litigation affecting how recognition is applied in practice.

The 2024 shift from the Indian Penal Code to the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita is a separate and additive source of risk: the gender-identity-specific offences that had given trans complainants a route into the criminal law disappeared with the old code, and communities report expecting a rise in assaults. A visitor weighing protection should not assume the pre-2024 complaint categories remain available.

Checkpoint and custody incidents are documented across several agencies rather than one force: the Railway Protection Force at stations and in Assam custody, CISF at an international airport terminal, and passport authorities requiring medical examination. The pattern spans rail, air and document issuance, which means screening friction can arise at more than one stage of a single journey.

Protection and hazard run side by side. The UK Home Office country note of December 2025 describes police abuse of LGBT+ people as limited and not systemic, while the Madras High Court's 2021 guidelines in S. Sushma v Commissioner of Police bind police conduct and bar conversion therapy. The same visitor who faces arbitrary screening may also have a court route open to them, which is a materially different posture from jurisdictions where no judicial remedy exists.
localsOnly:
Of the 487,803 transgender persons recorded in India's census, only about 32,500 hold identity cards, so the documentation gap was already wide before the March 2026 amendment added medical certification requirements.

Recognition under the amended scheme is tied to access to welfare schemes. The government frames the narrower, group-based definition as a mechanism for directing benefits and anti-trafficking protection, which means residents outside the recognised categories lose both the identity document and the scheme access attached to it.

Medical boards and district authorities hold the certification function for gender-affirming surgery, concentrating the administrative gatekeeping for residents in district-level machinery rather than in a self-declaration process.

Residents who support or accompany trans people face exposure under the new offence of coercing or alluring someone to be transgender, which Human Rights Watch has warned could reach support networks, families and activists.

Resident-facing remedies come from the courts rather than the statute: the Madras High Court's 7 June 2021 guidelines in S. Sushma v Commissioner of Police, delivered by Justice N. Anand Venkatesh, direct police sensitisation, prohibit conversion therapy and issue directions to the National Medical Commission and education authorities.
outOfScopeNotes:
Presidential assent to the March 2026 amendment was reported as pending in late March 2026. Whether it has since been assented to, challenged or stayed is unresolved in the sources available for this record.

No source in the inventory addresses Meghālaya specifically: no state-level legislation, no Meghalaya Police standing orders, no High Court of Meghalaya judgment and no local checkpoint incident. The absence reflects the sourcing, not a finding that Meghālaya differs from or matches the national position in any particular way.

The number of identity documents issued to residents of Meghālaya, and the presence of medical boards or district certification authorities in the state, are not sourced here.

Whether the March 2026 amendment applies to an entry visa, a visa-resident permit or an OCI-style document held by a trans visitor is not addressed in any available source; entry-document treatment for trans travellers is documented only through incident reports from other states.

The claim that trans communities anticipate a rise in assaults under the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita is a community report rather than a measured crime statistic; no post-2024 assault figures are available in this inventory.
